problem: Classical rule-based social navigation is interpretable and safe but hard to generalize, while RL needs heavy reward shaping and imitation learning suffers distribution shift and has no explicit safety mechanism.
motivation: Navigation among humans is safety-critical and must adapt to diverse human behaviors under real-time embedded constraints. The authors hypothesize that combining a data-driven reward learned from good and bad demonstrations with rule-based goal and obstacle terms gives a better adaptability-safety balance.
key_idea: Learn a kernel density-based reward from positive and negative demonstrations, add rule-based obstacle and goal rewards, use a sampling-based lookahead teacher on this reward, and distill it into an MDN student that outputs uncertainty.
insight: The ablation shows that removing the density reward causes the largest SR drop (99.4 to 83.0 in HR-RL, 99.6 to 79.8 in HL-RR), so demonstration-aligned rewards are essential in congested doorway interactions. The rule terms are complementary: dropping the goal term raises total time, and dropping the obstacle term lowers SR. The MDN student beats an MLP student, and its epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty is higher in risky frames (min human distance <0.8 m), so it can serve as a risk signal.
method: Density reward learning: RKHS reward over state-action pairs, maximizing expected reward under the empirical demonstration density with regularization; closed-form alpha=(lambda K_UU+beta I)^-1 (1/N_D) K_UD 1 with inducing points.
Smooth leveraged kernel: cos(pi/2 (gamma-gamma')) times a squared-exponential kernel, with gamma=+1 for positive and -1 for negative demonstrations, so unsafe samples lower reward.
Rule-based rewards: goal reward 1-tanh(d_goal/d_total) and obstacle reward tanh(mean nearest-obstacle clearance) over the rollout.
Adaptive weighting: alpha_den=1+cos(pi(1-r)), alpha_goal=2(1-r), alpha_obs=1, with r=clip(d_goal/d_total); the density reward dominates early and goal progress later.
Sampling-based lookahead teacher: 8 linear speeds (0.1-0.8 m/s) x 15 angular speeds in [-0.4pi,0.4pi]; 3 s horizon, dt 0.3 s, 10 Hz, EMA 0.5; picks the first action of the best rollout.

Uncertainty-aware distillation: DAgger (50 expert episodes, then 10 rounds x 50) into an MDN (2x128 hidden, K=10 mixtures) on a 29-D LiDAR observation; aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty via the law of total variance.

setting.backbone: Kernel density reward + sampling-based lookahead teacher; MDN student (2x128 MLP, 10 Gaussian components) trained by DAgger
setting.model_size: small MLP (2 hidden layers of 128 units)
setting.training_data: Keyboard-teleoperated demos: synthetic 446 positive / 337 negative; elevator HR-RL 732 positive / 170 negative; HL-RR 662 positive / 194 negative; plus DAgger rollouts labeled by the teacher
setting.observation: 2D LiDAR (72 beams grouped to 24 min-range features) + 2 nearest-obstacle distances and angles + relative goal angle (29-D)
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands [v, omega] (unicycle), teacher searches a discretized set
setting.simulator: custom 2D elevator co-boarding simulation with social-force humans (4x4 m map, Schindler 6000 geometry)
setting.privileged: Teacher uses forward simulation of future states (privileged); the student uses only observations

numbers.extra: trained on 732 positive / 170 negative demos; privileged forward simulation

numbers_note: Not a standard navigation benchmark; custom simulation. Real-world results are qualitative only.
results: In the elevator co-boarding simulation the teacher reaches about 99.4-99.6% SR versus CVaR-BF (72.8/71.4) and CrowdNav++ (78.6/64.8), with shorter paths. The distilled MDN student keeps 98.0-100% SR and beats the MLP student (95.8/98.8). Real-world trials with humans are shown qualitatively.
limitations: Human motion in simulation uses a social-force model, which does not capture real pedestrian variability
Fidelity gamma is restricted to binary +1/-1 labels rather than a continuous quality spectrum
Only a narrow elevator scenario with two baselines; the real-world evaluation is qualitative, without quantitative metrics
builds_on: Smooth leveraged kernel reward learning (Choi et al.)
